doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Bowie, airplay, Carla Bley, and Wynton's half-valve
summary: Bowie and Bley wanted airplay; Stewart recounts the 'Strange Fruit' starter pistol story and says Wynton borrows from Bowie.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Well I think, I would have conversations with him and I had conversations with Carla Bley about the same thing. I mean I listen to the jazz stations in New York, I hardly ever hear him play Carla Bley’s music. And she would complain, she’d say, “My stuff is really easy to listen to it’s just like this and this and this. I don’t understand what problem they have with it. Why don’t they play my music?” She would always get voted on in the polls and Down Beat things but very seldom would they play her music on the radio. And Lester felt some of that same frustration where he thought his music, even though he may have been known like Art Ensemble of Chicago which was kind of on the border and leaning on the music a little bit. A lot of the things we did with Brass Fantasy were really very palatable. And so he was trying to get some airplay. He wasn’t necessarily going all the way overboard because a lot of the arrangements, when we did them live, they would transcend “Saving All My Love” and become this whole other thing. Like we did one of Billie Holiday’s, “Strange Fruit” and it’s very emotional, very, very emotional. I mean even to the point of we were in Europe and we were on tour once and he bought a starter pistol and so when we got to the hanging part and the band kind of plays free for a period and he pulls out a starter — bang-bang-bang-bang-bang. People bailed out ducking or hitting the ground, it was hilarious. “Oh what are they doing, what are they doing?” You know what I mean? And then they would go back into the tune again and it’s like, but we did a bunch of stuff like that where he really does take “Saving All My Love” and lean on it. You know? Really lean on it. Or a lot of the tunes, Biggy Smalls’ tune and just lean on it and do stuff with it in terms of improvisation. Just like when he was asked to do the theme for the “Bill Cosby Show.” What he plays, he’s not trying to get airplay. You see what he’s playing is really abstract, but it works.
You know I didn’t even know that was him.
Now I’ve got to listen to it again.

That’s Lester Bowie playing that very [scats]. That’s him. As a matter of fact I listened to some of the things that Wynton’s doing now, more recently, and he’s doing Lester. I mean a lot of the things, as much as he may have objected at one point or another to Lester, the thing is when he’s doing a lot of his half-valve thing, he does a whole piece of half-valve, that’s Lester. There’s no other trumpet player that played like that. You know? So a lot of things that he’s doing, whether he wants to admit it or not, are admittedly coming out of Lester Bowie. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
